title: A universal AutoScore framework for predicting clinical outcomes
author: Xie, Ning, et al.

steps.title: Rank variables with AutoScore
steps.instruction: Run the ranking function on the training data. Use `AutoScore_rank(train_set = train_set, method = "rf", ntree = 100)` for binary outcomes (default). For AUC‑based ranking supply a validation set: `method = "auc", validation_set = validation_set`. For survival data use `AutoScore_rank_Survival()`, and for ordinal data use `AutoScore_rank_Ordinal()`. The command returns the variable ranking object (`ranking`).

steps.title: Create parsimony plot and select variables
steps.instruction: Generate a parsimony plot with the ranking result and choose the optimal number of variables. Call the appropriate function, e.g.: `AutoScore_parsimony(train_set = train_set, validation_set = validation_set, rank = ranking, max_score = 100, n_min = 1, n_max = 20, cross_validation = FALSE, fold = 10, categorize = "quantile", quantiles = c(0,0.05,0.2,0.8,0.95,1), max_cluster = 5, do_trace = FALSE, auc_lim_min = 0.5, auc_lim_max = "adaptive", link = "logit")`. For survival outcomes use `AutoScore_parsimony_Survival()`, for ordinal outcomes use `AutoScore_parsimony_Ordinal()` (link argument may be changed but must be consistent later). Examine the plot, decide on `num_var` (e.g., 6), and extract the final variable list: `final_variables <- names(ranking[1:num_var])`.

steps.title: Generate initial cutoffs and scoring table
steps.instruction: Create initial cutoff values for all continuous variables and obtain the first scoring table. Run: `cut_vec <- AutoScore_weighting(train_set = train_set, validation_set = validation_set, final_variables = final_variables, max_score = 100, categorize = "quantile", quantiles = c(0,0.05,0.2,0.8,0.95,1), metrics_ci = FALSE, time_point = NULL, n_boot = 100, link = "logit")`. For survival data use `AutoScore_weighting_Survival()` and supply `time_point`; for ordinal data use `AutoScore_weighting_Ordinal()` and supply `link`. The function returns `cut_vec` and an intermediate `scoring_table` together with performance metrics (ROC/AUC for binary, iAUC for survival, mAUC for ordinal). If performance is unsatisfactory, return to step 2 to adjust the variable list.

steps.title: Fine‑tune cutoffs and scoring table
steps.instruction: Optionally modify the automatically generated cut‑offs (e.g., `cut_vec$Age`, `cut_vec$Lab_H`, etc.) to clinically meaningful values, then re‑train the score: `scoring_table <- AutoScore_fine_tuning(train_set = train_set, validation_set = validation_set, final_variables = final_variables, cut_vec = cut_vec, max_score = 100, metrics_ci = FALSE, time_point = NULL, n_boot = 100, report_cindex = FALSE, link = "logit")`. Use the survival‑ or ordinal‑specific versions (`AutoScore_fine_tuning_Survival()`, `AutoScore_fine_tuning_Ordinal()`) when appropriate, adding `time_point` or `link` arguments as required. The function outputs an updated `scoring_table` and performance measures. Repeat fine‑tuning until the intermediate results are satisfactory.

steps.title: Evaluate final score on test set
steps.instruction: Apply the finalized scoring system to an independent test dataset. Run the testing function: `pred_score <- AutoScore_testing(test_set = test_set, final_variables = final_variables, cut_vec = cut_vec, scoring_table = scoring_table, threshold = "best", with_label = TRUE, metrics_ci = FALSE, time_point = NULL, n_boot = 100, report_cindex = FALSE, link = "logit")`. For binary outcomes you may also use a fixed threshold, e.g., `threshold = 90`. Then print performance: `print_roc_performance(pred_score$Label, pred_score$pred_score, threshold = 90)`. For survival data use `AutoScore_testing_Survival()` (add `time_point`), and for ordinal data use `AutoScore_testing_Ordinal()` (add `link`). The command returns predicted scores and final performance metrics (ROC/AUC, iAUC, mAUC, optional c‑index).

description: Scoring systems are widely used in clinical settings for the convenient assessment of individual risk and may provide an easy-to-use tool to underpin clinical decision-making.4,5,6,7 For example, the well-known Framingham hypertension risk score uses seven routinely collected variables to identify high-risk patients for early intervention and efficient management, including lifestyle change programs and blood pressure-lowering treatment.8,9 The LACE index10 uses basic information on current inpatient stay, previous visits to emergency departments and comorbidity to identify patients with an elevated risk of adverse outcomes post-discharge for additional care. With the increased availability of data and analytical tools, there have been ongoing efforts to update existing scores11 and to devise new clinical risk scores for a wide range of clinical applications.4,12 Scoring systems are inherently easily interpretable, as they represent linear classification models that only require users to add, subtract and multiply a few numbers to make a prediction.13 The facile interpretability may support clinical decision-making, where doctors can easily understand in which risk category an individual patient falls.14,15,16,17 Compared with complex post-hoc explanations in machine learning, clinicians prefer intrinsically interpretable and transparent models, especially those used at the bedside.18,19,20,21 AutoScore1 was developed as an interpretable machine learning-based automatic clinical score generator. The framework consists of six modules: (1) variable ranking with machine learning, (2) variable transformation, (3) score derivation, (4) model selection, (5) domain knowledge-based score fine-tuning, and (6) performance evaluation.
